title: Why Do We Still Have Ancient NIGHTMARES?
title_alternatives: Why Your Nightmares Are 100,000 Years Old
Why Do We Dream About Being CHASED?
What Were Ancient Humans' Nightmares About?
Your Brain Still Thinks Lions Are Hunting You
The Ancient Reason You Have Bad Dreams
description:
Why do so many of us dream about being chased, falling or hiding in the dark - even though most of us have never met a wild predator? In this video we look at the threat simulation theory of dreaming, what happens in the brain during REM sleep, how hunter-gatherer groups share the night watch, and why a stressful week can end with an ancient-looking nightmare.

This is an animated explainer, not medical advice. If nightmares are affecting your sleep often, please talk to a doctor.

Sources:
sources: Revonsuo, A. (2000). The reinterpretation of dreams: An evolutionary hypothesis of the function of dreaming. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 23(6).
Nielsen, T. A. et al. (2003). The Typical Dreams of Canadian University Students. Dreaming, 13(4).
Valli, K. et al. (2005). The threat simulation theory of the evolutionary function of dreaming: Evidence from dreams of traumatized children. Consciousness and Cognition, 14(1).
Samson, D. R. et al. (2017). Chronotype variation drives night-time sentinel-like behaviour in hunter-gatherers. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 284.
Walker, M. P. & van der Helm, E. (2009). Overnight therapy? The role of sleep in emotional brain processing. Psychological Bulletin, 135(5).
Krakow, B. et al. (2001). Imagery rehearsal therapy for chronic nightmares in sexual assault survivors with PTSD. JAMA, 286(5).

scenes.narration: It's 3 a.m. You're running, but your legs feel like wet sand. Something is right behind you. And then you wake up.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character running in slow motion through a dark forest at night, terrified face, glowing eyes in the bushes behind him

scenes.narration: Here's the weird part: whatever chased you probably wasn't a boss or a tax bill. It was something with teeth. Why?
scenes.image_prompt: the main character sitting up in a modern bed, sweating, a thought bubble above him showing a shadowy creature with big teeth

scenes.narration: Your brain lives in a world of Wi-Fi and pizza delivery, but at night it still seems to rehearse a much older world.
scenes.image_prompt: split scene: left side a cozy modern bedroom with a phone charging, right side a dark prehistoric cave with a campfire

scenes.narration: To understand why, we have to go back, way back, to the people who slept on the ground with nothing between them and the dark.
scenes.image_prompt: a group of stick-figure ancient humans lying on grass around a small fire under a huge starry sky

scenes.narration: First, a quick fact. Being chased is one of the most common dream themes ever recorded, across countries and age groups.
scenes.image_prompt: a big world map with little stick figures in different countries all running from shadows, arrows pointing everywhere

scenes.narration: In one large survey of university students, being chased or pursued came out near the very top of the list.
scenes.image_prompt: a classroom of stick-figure students raising hands, a bar chart on the board with the tallest bar showing a running figure

scenes.narration: Falling, being late, losing teeth, being attacked. Different lives, weirdly similar nightmares.
scenes.image_prompt: four small panels: a figure falling off a cliff, a figure running for a clock, a figure holding a tooth, a figure hiding from a shadow

scenes.narration: So is your brain just random at night? Some scientists think it's doing something surprisingly useful.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character tapping his head, a cartoon brain with a tiny hard hat working at a desk inside it

scenes.narration: In 2000, a Finnish researcher named Antti Revonsuo proposed an idea called the threat simulation theory.
scenes.image_prompt: a friendly stick-figure scientist with glasses standing next to a chalkboard that shows a drawing of a figure dodging a lion

scenes.narration: The idea is simple: dreams may work like a flight simulator for danger.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character sitting in a wooden cockpit-style simulator made of sticks, a screen showing a charging mammoth

scenes.narration: A pilot practices engine failures in a simulator so a real emergency feels a little familiar. Your brain may do the same with threats.
scenes.image_prompt: side by side: a pilot in a simulator and the main character dreaming, both calmly pressing buttons while alarms flash

scenes.narration: For our ancestors, the threats were very real. Big cats, wolves, snakes, falling from rocks, and sometimes other humans.
scenes.image_prompt: a prehistoric landscape with a big cat on a rock, a snake in the grass, a wolf pack in the distance, the main character looking worried

scenes.narration: A person who had already rehearsed running, hiding or climbing, even only in a dream, might react a split second faster.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character quickly climbing a tree while a big cat looks up disappointed

scenes.narration: And in the wild, a split second could decide who became an ancestor and who became dinner.
scenes.image_prompt: two stick figures: one safely up in a tree waving, the other sitting inside a comically large cat's shadow outline

scenes.narration: Now, this is a theory, not a proven fact. But there are some interesting clues that fit it.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character as a detective with a magnifying glass looking at footprints labeled only with question marks shapes

scenes.narration: Clue number one: when researchers collect children's dreams, animals show up much more often than in adult dreams.
scenes.image_prompt: a small stick-figure child sleeping with a thought bubble full of cartoon animals: bear, wolf, snake, big cat

scenes.narration: Many of those dream animals are not the cat or dog at home. They're wild, big and often threatening.
scenes.image_prompt: the child's dream bubble zooms in: a huge bear towering over a tiny house cat that looks confused

scenes.narration: It's a bit strange. Most kids today have never met a wolf, yet wolves still find their way into bedtime nightmares.
scenes.image_prompt: a modern child's bedroom with posters and toys, a cartoon wolf peeking from under the bed

scenes.narration: Clue number two comes from children who grew up in genuinely dangerous places.
scenes.image_prompt: a serious scene: a small village at dusk with smoke in the distance, a child looking up at the sky

scenes.narration: A study of children living through war found they reported more threatening dreams than children living in peaceful areas.
scenes.image_prompt: two groups of stick-figure children sleeping, one group with many dark dream bubbles, the other with calmer dream bubbles

scenes.narration: That fits the idea that the dream simulator switches on more often when the real world feels dangerous.
scenes.image_prompt: a big cartoon switch on a brain labeled with a lightning bolt icon being flipped up, warning lights turning on

scenes.narration: Clue number three is about how dreams are built inside the brain during REM sleep.
scenes.image_prompt: a cartoon brain lying in a tiny bed under a blanket, eyes darting left and right under closed eyelids

scenes.narration: During REM sleep, the amygdala, a brain area strongly linked to fear and emotion, is very active.
scenes.image_prompt: a cartoon brain with one small almond-shaped area glowing bright red like an alarm bell

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, parts of the front of the brain that normally say 'calm down, that makes no sense' are much quieter.
scenes.image_prompt: a tiny sleepy stick figure at the front of the brain wearing a nightcap, snoring, while an alarm rings behind him

scenes.narration: Alarm on, fact-checker asleep. No wonder a normal hallway can turn into a monster chase.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character in a long glowing hallway at night, doors turning into mouths with teeth, a comic sweat drop on his head

scenes.narration: But why would evolution keep such an uncomfortable feature? To answer that, let's look at how ancient people actually slept.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character scratching his head next to a big question mark made of sticks, a moon in the sky

scenes.narration: Researchers have studied modern hunter-gatherer and small farming groups, like the Hadza in Tanzania, to learn about natural sleep.
scenes.image_prompt: a small camp of grass huts under acacia trees at night, a few stick figures sleeping, one sitting by a fire

scenes.narration: They found something surprising: in one Hadza study, over about three weeks, everyone was asleep at the same time for only around eighteen minutes.
scenes.image_prompt: a camp at night with many sleeping figures and always one figure awake by the fire, a small clock icon showing a short time

scenes.narration: Someone was almost always awake. Night owls, early birds and light sleepers took turns without planning it.
scenes.image_prompt: a row of stick figures: an owl-hatted one awake late, a rooster-hatted one awake early, one tossing and turning

scenes.narration: Scientists call this the sentinel idea. A group with mixed sleep habits has a built-in night watch.
scenes.image_prompt: a stick-figure guard with a spear standing proudly on a rock while the rest of the group sleeps behind him

scenes.narration: And if you're the one half-awake at 3 a.m., a brain that jumps quickly into alarm mode might actually be helpful.
scenes.image_prompt: the guard's eyes wide open, a rustle in the bushes shown with motion lines, the guard ready to shout

scenes.narration: Here's my honest take: I don't think nightmares were designed to torture us. They look more like an old smoke alarm that is a little too sensitive.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character looking straight at the viewer, pointing at a smoke alarm on the ceiling that is beeping at a slice of toast

scenes.narration: A smoke alarm that goes off for burnt toast is annoying. A smoke alarm that stays silent during a real fire is deadly.
scenes.image_prompt: split scene: left a kitchen with burnt toast and a beeping alarm and an annoyed figure, right a silent alarm with flames and a shocked figure

scenes.narration: Evolution usually prefers the annoying alarm. False alarms cost you sleep. Missed alarms could cost you everything.
scenes.image_prompt: a balance scale: on one side a pillow, on the other a skull-free cartoon danger sign, the danger side much heavier

scenes.narration: Now here's the modern twist. The alarm system is still installed, but the threats around us have completely changed.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character in a modern office surrounded by emails, deadlines and a ringing phone, looking stressed

scenes.narration: Most of us will never be chased by a big cat. But we do get chased by exams, deadlines and awkward conversations.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character running from a giant flying stack of papers and a calendar with teeth

scenes.narration: And the old brain seems to translate modern stress into ancient pictures: being chased, falling, hiding, being attacked.
scenes.image_prompt: a cartoon translation machine: a stressful email goes in one side, a charging mammoth comes out the other side

scenes.narration: That's why a stressful week can end with a dream about running through a forest you have never seen.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character asleep at a desk with a laptop, dream bubble showing him running through an ancient forest

scenes.narration: There's also a second, gentler idea about what dreams do: they may help us process emotions.
scenes.image_prompt: a warm scene: the main character sitting by a calm river at sunset, thought bubbles floating away like leaves

scenes.narration: Some sleep researchers describe REM sleep as a kind of overnight therapy.
scenes.image_prompt: a cartoon brain lying on a therapist's couch, a friendly moon in a cardigan taking notes

scenes.narration: The idea is that we replay emotional memories while stress chemicals in the brain are unusually low, so the sting slowly fades.
scenes.image_prompt: a memory shown as a spiky red ball being gently washed in a moonlit stream and becoming smooth and blue

scenes.narration: In that view, a bad dream can be the brain trying to file away something scary, but the process doesn't always go smoothly.
scenes.image_prompt: a messy filing cabinet in a brain with folders flying out, a tiny stick-figure clerk struggling to close the drawer

scenes.narration: These two ideas don't fight each other. Dreams might both rehearse danger and help us calm down after it.
scenes.image_prompt: two cartoon brains shaking hands, one wearing a helmet, the other holding a cup of tea

scenes.narration: Now, an important reality check. Having nightmares now and then is completely normal.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character giving a thumbs up, a calendar showing only a few small cloud icons across a month

scenes.narration: Surveys suggest most adults have an occasional bad dream, and kids tend to have them more often than adults.
scenes.image_prompt: a group of stick figures of different ages, the smaller ones with slightly more dream clouds above their heads

scenes.narration: But for a smaller group of people, nightmares happen so often that they wreck sleep and daily life.
scenes.image_prompt: a tired stick figure with dark circles under the eyes holding a huge coffee mug, many dark clouds above

scenes.narration: That can happen after trauma, during very stressful periods, or with some medicines. And it's something doctors can actually help with.
scenes.image_prompt: a friendly stick-figure doctor with a stethoscope talking kindly to a tired patient in a bright clinic

scenes.narration: One well-studied approach is called imagery rehearsal therapy, and it sounds almost too simple.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character holding a pencil over a notebook with a small drawing of a monster, curious expression

scenes.narration: While awake, you write down a recurring nightmare, change the ending into something less scary, and practice the new version.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character redrawing a monster in his notebook into a small silly monster wearing a party hat

scenes.narration: In other words, you give your ancient flight simulator a new script. For many people, that reduces how often the nightmare returns.
scenes.image_prompt: the wooden simulator from earlier, its screen now showing the mammoth tripping over and everyone laughing

scenes.narration: It's kind of beautiful. The same system that learned from rehearsal can be calmed down by rehearsal.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character smiling peacefully in bed, the moon outside the window smiling back

scenes.narration: Let's go back to the campfire for a moment.
scenes.image_prompt: the ancient camp at night again, a warm glowing fire in the center, stars above

scenes.narration: Imagine an ancient teenager waking up from a dream about a lion, heart pounding, and moving a little closer to the fire.
scenes.image_prompt: a young stick figure sitting up suddenly in the grass, then scooting closer to the fire and to the group

scenes.narration: That small reaction, moving closer to the group, staying alert, listening to the night, might have made a real difference over thousands of years.
scenes.image_prompt: the young figure sitting near the guard, both listening, the bushes nearby perfectly still

scenes.narration: Nobody knows exactly how much dreams shaped human survival. But the pattern is hard to ignore.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character standing in front of a long timeline from caves to cities, shrugging with a thoughtful face

scenes.narration: The most common nightmares still look like the dangers our ancestors faced every day: being hunted, falling, being alone in the dark.
scenes.image_prompt: three glowing cave paintings on a rock wall: a figure being chased, a figure falling, a figure alone under the moon

scenes.narration: So the next time you wake up from a dream about being chased, try a different thought than 'what's wrong with me?'
scenes.image_prompt: the main character waking up in a modern bed, taking a deep breath, a small thought bubble with a question mark

scenes.narration: Maybe it's just a very old part of you running a fire drill. Loudly. At the worst possible time.
scenes.image_prompt: a tiny caveman version of the main character inside his head banging on a drum with a fire-drill sign

scenes.narration: And here's what I find comforting: that system exists because someone, long ago, survived the night.
scenes.image_prompt: a warm sunrise over the ancient camp, all the stick figures waking up safely and stretching

scenes.narration: Every nightmare is a strange little echo of ancestors who were careful enough, lucky enough, or scared enough to make it to morning.
scenes.image_prompt: a long line of faint ghostly stick-figure ancestors standing behind the main character, all smiling and waving

scenes.narration: Of course, you don't live in a camp surrounded by lions. So it's okay to tell your inner alarm: thanks, but I've got this.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character patting a small nervous cartoon alarm bell on the head, the bell calming down

scenes.narration: A regular sleep time, less doom-scrolling before bed and a calm routine can make that old alarm a lot less jumpy.
scenes.image_prompt: a cozy bedroom at night with the phone placed away on a shelf, a book and a warm lamp on the nightstand

scenes.narration: And if nightmares are wrecking your sleep week after week, talking to a doctor is a smart move, not an overreaction.
scenes.image_prompt: the friendly doctor from before giving the main character a thumbs up in a bright clinic

scenes.narration: So, why do we still have ancient nightmares? Because our brains are older than our cities.
scenes.image_prompt: a modern city skyline at night with a huge faint outline of an ancient cave drawn behind it

scenes.narration: We upgraded our homes, our tools and our phones, but at night we still sleep with a mind shaped by campfires.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character in modern pajamas lying in bed, his shadow on the wall shaped like a caveman beside a fire

scenes.narration: If you had to guess, what was the most common thing chasing you in your own dreams? Tell me in the comments.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character looking at the viewer with a curious smile, holding a small sign with a question mark

scenes.narration: And if you want to know how ancient humans slept, ate, or survived the cold, there's another story waiting for you right next to this one.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character walking toward a glowing doorway that shows a snowy prehistoric landscape

scenes.narration: Sleep well. And if something chases you tonight, remember: your ancestors outran it first.
scenes.image_prompt: the main character sleeping peacefully while a tiny cartoon mammoth tiptoes quietly past the window under the moon
